Underneath all of it, the colour discipline does the real work: the background, the surface and the gelato are all versions of one green, so the dark chocolate is the only dark thing in the frame and the eye goes straight to the swirl. The camera is low, so the pan is seen from below its rim line and reads as monumental.

FRAMING AND CAMERA — Aspect ratio 4:5, vertical. One pan, centred, its vertical axis at about half the frame width. Including its body it spans about six tenths of the frame height: the far edge of its rim at about one quarter of the frame height, its near rim at about seven tenths, and the bottom of its body at about five sixths. Its rim is about six tenths of the frame width. The surface it stands on meets the background in a soft horizontal transition at about forty-five hundredths of the frame height, so the pan's upper rim rises above that line and its body sits below it. The heaped bed of ingredients surrounds the base, running across the frame from the left edge to the right edge and continuing past both, its front spilling forward to about nine tenths of the frame height. The falling ingredients occupy the upper half of the frame, spread on both sides of the pan and above it, several cropped by the top edge and by both side edges. Lens 85mm, camera low — about thirty-five degrees above the plane of the surface — so the gelato's worked surface is seen at a steep raking angle, the pan is strongly foreshortened and narrower at the back than the front, and the near rim and the front wall of the pan are both visible. Aperture f/7.1.

HERO EFFECT ONE — THE SURFACE OF THE GELATO. Two materials in direct contact, and the picture depends on them behaving in opposite ways.

The gelato is dense and completely matte. It scatters light rather than reflecting it, so it has no highlight anywhere — only broad soft gradations that follow its shape. It has been worked with a spatula into soft rounded folds, ridges and low peaks that run irregularly across the tray, with drag marks visible where the blade passed and small trapped air cells showing at the cut edges. Its colour is a pale creamy yellow-green, lighter on the lifted ridges and deepening in the crevices between them, and it varies slightly across the tray rather than being one flat tone.

The chocolate is the opposite: a broad ribbon of dark chocolate laid over and through the gelato, and it is a true glossy surface. It carries wide soft bright reflections along its curves and drops to near-black in its troughs, with a thin sharp bright line running along every edge where the chocolate thins out. It has flowed rather than been cut, so its outline is lobed and rounded with soft bays and tongues, thicker where it pooled and translucent-thin where it ran. It wanders across the tray in an irregular meandering band, doubling back on itself, wide in places and narrow in others, and in several areas it has been folded into the gelato so that pale green and dark brown marble together in thin swirls. Scattered through those marbled areas are small chopped chocolate flecks, matte where they are freshly broken. Nowhere is the ribbon symmetrical or evenly spaced, and nowhere does the gelato take on the chocolate's gloss.

HERO EFFECT TWO — THE FALLING INGREDIENTS. Nuts and broken chocolate pieces suspended in the air above and around the pan, and their conviction depends on four things. They sit at clearly different distances from the lens: the furthest are small and slightly soft, the middle ones are at natural size and sharp, and two or three nearest the lens are noticeably larger and clearly out of focus, their outlines spread. They are all turned differently — every nut at its own rotation, every chocolate shard showing a different face, none of them presented squarely and none repeating another's angle. They are distributed unevenly: they cluster more densely directly above the pan where they are falling from, thin out toward the sides, and leave whole areas of the background empty; they never sit at equal spacing and never form an arc or a line. And they are lit from the same direction as the pan, so the light on each piece agrees with the light on the product — that is what stops them reading as pasted cut-outs. Each is frozen sharp rather than streaked: this is a short-duration exposure, not a long one, and nothing in the air is dragged or smeared. A fine scatter of small crumbs and dust falls among the larger pieces.

PROPS AND OBJECTS — The pan is a rectangular stainless steel gastronorm tray with rounded corners and a rolled outer rim. Brushed steel is not a full mirror: its flat faces return a soft, slightly streaky reflection with fine parallel brushing marks running along them, picking up the green of the surroundings so the metal carries a green cast across its broad areas. Its rolled rim is the exception — the tight curve there concentrates light into a continuous hard bright band running all the way around the top of the pan, with a dark band immediately beneath it, and this rim highlight is the brightest thing in the picture. A small embossed marking is pressed into the rim, low in contrast and reading as shape rather than as legible text. Shelled pistachio kernels heaped around the base: each is split along its natural seam, its papery skin a mottled purple-tan that has rubbed away in patches to show the green kernel beneath, and every one differs in size, in colour and in how much skin remains. They are completely matte and take no highlight. A few still carry a fragment of shell. Broken chocolate chunks scattered among them: each shard has a smooth moulded face that is glossy and reflects light, and freshly fractured faces that are matte, paler and finely granular — that difference between the two faces on the same piece is what makes broken chocolate read as broken rather than cut. Their edges are sharp and angular, and no two pieces are the same shape or size. Around and between them, a scatter of fine ground nut crumb and chocolate dust, denser near the pan and thinning outward, clustered irregularly rather than sprinkled evenly.

LIGHTING — A single hard source placed high and to the right and slightly behind, raking down across the scene. Because it is hard, every element casts a defined shadow: the pan lays a clear shadow across the surface to the left, each falling piece is modelled on one side and dark on the other, and every nut and chocolate shard in the heap casts its own small crisp shadow down and to the left, so the bed reads as a three-dimensional pile rather than a flat texture. The rolled rim of the pan carries the brightest highlight in the frame. The chocolate ribbon's reflections come next. The gelato sits about a stop below them and holds no highlight at all. The background carries a soft brighter wedge on the right where the light spills onto it, falling off to about two stops down at the left edge and the upper left corner. The heaped bed sits about a stop and a half below the gelato. Every transition curves with the surface it crosses; nothing is straight-edged. The lighting sets brightness and falloff only.

BACKGROUND AND SURFACE — A plain deep saturated green backdrop, unbroken, with no seam, texture, object or mark anywhere on it, matte so it holds no sheen. It meets a surface of the same deep green in a soft horizontal transition rather than a hard line. The surface is matte and slightly darker than the backdrop, absorbing light and returning no reflection, so the shadows on it read cleanly. Nothing else is in the frame: no scoop, no cone, no second pan, no cloth, no styling prop. Depth is carried by five separations at five distances: the nearest falling pieces, the front of the heaped bed, the pan, the further falling pieces, and the background.

FOCUS — Depth-of-field blur only, no motion blur anywhere; every edge is a still edge and nothing in the air is streaked. Critical sharpness sits on the near rim of the pan and the front third of the gelato surface — the spatula marks, the air cells, the sharp edges of the chocolate ribbon and its reflections are all fully resolved there. The far end of the pan is slightly soft, and so are the nuts immediately behind it. The nuts and chocolate at the very front of the heap, being closest to the lens, are noticeably soft while their shapes stay completely readable. Among the falling pieces, those at the pan's own distance are sharp, those further back are slightly soft and smaller, and the two or three nearest the lens are clearly out of focus and larger. The background is smooth and entirely off the plane of sharpness.

COLOUR — A single-hue picture with one dark counterpoint. Everything in the frame except the chocolate and the steel is a version of green: the background a deep saturated green, the surface a slightly darker green, the gelato a pale creamy yellow-green, the nut kernels a muted green under mottled purple-tan skins. Against that, the chocolate is a deep near-black brown and is the only dark value in the picture — it must stay brown-black and never drift toward grey or purple. The steel is neutral but picks up the green of its surroundings in its broad reflections while its rim highlight stays neutral white. There is no blue, no orange and no red anywhere in the frame, and the green must stay saturated and clean rather than going grey or olive.

CAPTURE — A real exposure made on a medium-format camera with studio strobe at a short duration. Light falls off toward the four corners, the upper left darkest. The rim highlight on the pan and the brightest points on the chocolate ribbon clip hard and stay narrow; the lit crests of the gelato clip softly and keep their modelling. Shadows stay open — the heaped bed holds readable detail in its shadowed gaps rather than collapsing to black, and the darkest corner of the background sits above pure black. Every repeated element varies: no two nuts the same size, colour or amount of remaining skin, no two chocolate shards the same shape, no two falling pieces at the same angle or the same distance, no two ridges of gelato alike, and none of them evenly spaced. Very slight fine grain throughout, a little heavier in the darker green of the background.

FINAL CHECK — One steel gelato pan, alone, centred and spanning about six tenths of the frame height, its base buried in a heaped bed of nuts and broken chocolate that crosses both side edges of the frame, on a deep green surface against a deep green background with nothing else in the picture. The camera is low, about thirty-five degrees above the surface, so the gelato is seen at a raking angle and the pan is strongly foreshortened. Nuts and chocolate pieces are suspended in the air at different distances, different sizes and different degrees of sharpness, unevenly spread and none touching the pan, all frozen and none streaked. The gelato is completely matte and the chocolate ribbon is glossy — the two must never share the same surface. Do not raise the camera to look down into the pan, do not tidy the heaped bed into an even ring, and do not space the falling pieces evenly.

title: Refrescante Smoothie de Morango e Limão
description: Um smoothie vibrante de morango e limão em copo descartável, com frutas frescas e gelo flutuando ao redor, evocando frescor e sabor.
prompt:
SWAP SLOT 1 — THE DRINK AND THE CUP. Image 1 is the product reference. Take from it only the physical object: the shape and proportions of the cup and its lid, the material and clarity of the plastic, the colour, opacity and layering of the drink inside, the garnish sitting under the dome, and any printed mark on the cup exactly as printed. Take nothing else from image 1 — not its background, not its surface, not its lighting, not its shadows, not its colour grade, and not any prop beside it. The product is placed into the scene described below and lit by the lights described below. The text below never invents any lettering.

SWAP SLOT 2 — THE FLYING INGREDIENTS. As written, the ingredients suspended in the air are whole strawberries, lime slices, mint leaves and ice cubes. They must always match what is in the drink. To change the drink, change these too, but keep the composition and the material logic identical: roughly six pieces of the main fruit at four different distances, two pieces of a second fruit cut to show its interior, two or three fresh leaves, and three or four ice cubes. Whatever is substituted must be described the same way — by what its surface does to light, not by its name. A whole fruit gets its skin and its sheen; a cut piece gets its internal structure and its translucency; a leaf gets its veins and its cuticle; ice gets its fractures and its refraction. An ingredient named without its optical behaviour comes back looking like plastic.

THE PICTURE — A vertical commercial drink photograph: one clear plastic cup with a domed lid, full of a layered blended fruit drink, standing on a white surface against a plain pale grey background, with whole fruit, cut fruit, fresh leaves and ice cubes suspended in the air all around it, frozen mid-flight.

THE READING — This is an advertising image and it is built on one impossible fact: the ingredients are floating. That impossibility is the energy of the picture, and it only works if the suspension is convincing — each piece at a different distance from the lens, at a different angle, at a different size and at a different degree of sharpness, so the eye reads a volume of space around the cup rather than a flat collage of cut-outs pasted around it. The ingredients are also the recipe: every raw component of the drink appears whole in the air, so the viewer reads what is in the cup at a glance. The ground is empty white and pale grey with no context of any kind, so the product is the only content. And the cup itself is transparent, which is the point — the layering inside is the proof of what was blended, and it must be visible.

FRAMING AND CAMERA — Aspect ratio 4:5, vertical. The cup stands centred, its vertical axis at about half the frame width. Including the dome lid it spans about seven tenths of the frame height: the top of the dome at about one fifth of the frame height, the base of the cup at about nine tenths. Its body is about four tenths of the frame width. The surface it stands on meets the background in a soft horizontal transition at about seven tenths of the frame height, so the lower three tenths of the picture is tabletop and the upper seven tenths is background. The suspended ingredients occupy the space around the cup and are placed unevenly: several are cropped by the frame edges and continue past them — one at the top edge, one at the left edge at mid-height, two at the right edge, and one at the bottom left corner. None of them touches the cup and none overlaps the front face of the cup, so the drink inside is never obscured. Lens 85mm, camera at about two thirds of the cup's height, held perfectly level with no tilt, so the dome lid is seen very slightly from above and the cup's sides stay parallel. Aperture f/5.6.

HERO EFFECT ONE — THE SUSPENSION. The ingredients hang in mid-air, and the picture succeeds or fails on how convincingly they occupy depth. Four rules govern them all. They sit at four clearly different distances from the lens: the furthest are small and slightly soft, the middle ones are at their natural size and critically sharp, and the nearest — the one at the bottom left corner — is noticeably larger than the others and clearly out of focus, with its outline and highlights spread. They are all turned differently: no two pieces of the same fruit are at the same rotation, none is presented squarely face-on, and several are seen at oblique angles that partly foreshorten them. They are spread unevenly around the cup: some cluster within a hand's width of each other and other areas of the frame are left empty, and none of them sit at equal spacing or on any regular arc. And each casts no shadow on anything and touches nothing, but each is lit from the same direction as the cup, so the light on every piece agrees with the light on the product — this is what stops them reading as pasted cut-outs. Their orientations are plausible for objects in flight: tilted, tumbling, some with their leaves trailing, none standing perfectly upright.

HERO EFFECT TWO — THE DRINK IN THE CUP. Seen through clear plastic, the contents are layered and irregular. The main body is a blended fruit slush: opaque rather than transparent, a deep saturated red-pink, and granular — its surface against the inside wall shows fine pulp texture, tiny paler seed specks scattered through it unevenly, and small trapped air bubbles pressed flat against the plastic. Through that red run pale cream-white streaks, swirled rather than layered flatly, and across the middle third of the cup a band of pale green: thin rounds of cut lime pressed against the inside wall, their segment structure and pale radial membranes visible through the plastic, slightly softened and displaced sideways by the refraction of the wall. Small dark green flecks of crushed leaf are scattered through the paler band. The boundaries between red, cream and green are irregular and marbled, never horizontal lines. Near the top the mixture rises to a slightly domed surface just below the lid. On the outside of the cup, a fine condensation: small separate beads rather than a sheet, denser and larger toward the base and sparse near the rim, each bead a tiny lens with a bright rim, a darker core and one small hard specular on top, varying in size and clustering irregularly.

PROPS AND OBJECTS — The cup is thin clear PET: glossy, so where its curved wall turns away from the lens it concentrates light into two bright vertical bands running the height of the cup, one on each side, and everything seen through it is refracted — shifted and compressed rather than seen through as if it were a window. Its rim is a thicker rolled band that catches a bright continuous line, and its base is a moulded ring that pools a brighter patch of light where it meets the surface. The lid is a clear domed cap snapped over the rim with a ridged flange: the dome is a strong curved reflector, carrying one large soft bright reflection across its upper left and a thinner one on its right, and beneath it sit garnishes — a halved fruit showing its cut face, a wedge of citrus, and a fresh leaf sprig — seen through the plastic slightly softened and slightly displaced. Whole strawberries: deep glossy red skin with a broad soft highlight on the shoulder of each, their seeds sitting in small dimples so each seed has a tiny shadow beside it, and a crisp green calyx whose leaves are thin enough to be semi-translucent at their tips. Lime pieces cut to show the interior: the flesh is translucent so light passes through it and the segments glow from within, their membranes reading as pale radial lines, a ring of opaque white pith around them and a thin green rind whose surface is pitted with small oil glands, each pit a tiny shadowed dimple. Mint leaves: saturated green, cupped rather than flat, their upper surface a waxy cuticle laying one broad soft sheen along the leaf, their raised veins branching irregularly and reading darker against the lit lamina, their serrated edges catching thin bright lines. Ice cubes: clear hard-edged blocks, each with sharp bright edges where the light concentrates, internal fracture planes reading as pale sheets inside the block, a cloudier core, and a bright caustic patch where light has been focused through and out the far side — and each cube is slightly different in size and in how far it has begun to round off at its corners. Beneath the cup, a plain white surface, matte, returning a soft diffuse reflection of the cup's base rather than a mirror image.

LIGHTING — A large soft source placed high and forward and slightly to the left, plus a second broad fill on the right, so the cup and every floating object are lit from the same directions with soft, open modelling and no hard shadow anywhere. The light passes through the translucent items — the cut citrus, the leaf edges, the ice — so they glow from within and are brighter than the opaque items beside them. The two vertical bands on the cup's wall and the reflection on the dome are the brightest areas on the product. The drink inside sits about a stop below them. Beneath the cup, a soft grey contact shadow spreads across the white surface, darkest and tightest directly under the base and softening quickly outward, anchoring the cup to the table. The background is brightest in a broad pool behind the cup and falls off gently toward the top corners and the upper edges, ending about a stop and a half down. Every transition curves with the surface it crosses; nothing is straight-edged. The lighting sets brightness and falloff only.

BACKGROUND — A plain seamless studio background in a very pale cool grey, curving without a visible edge into a white tabletop, so the transition between them is a soft horizontal gradient rather than a line. The surface is matte with no texture, seam, object or mark anywhere on it. Nothing else is in the frame: no splash, no spill, no straw, no second cup, no garnish resting on the table. Depth is carried by five separations at five distances: the nearest floating item at the bottom left, the mid-distance floating items, the cup, the further floating items, and the background.

FOCUS — Depth-of-field blur only, no motion blur anywhere; every edge is a still edge and no flying object is streaked or dragged. Critical sharpness sits on the front face of the cup — the condensation beads, the pulp texture, the seed specks and the lime segments pressed against the inside wall are all fully resolved — and carries through the dome lid and the garnish beneath it. The floating items at the cup's own distance are equally sharp, with individual strawberry seeds, leaf veins and the fracture planes inside the ice all resolved. Items further back are slightly soft and slightly smaller. The single item at the bottom left corner is much closer to the lens, noticeably larger, and clearly out of focus, its colour and shape still completely readable. The background is smooth and entirely off the plane of sharpness.

COLOUR — A clean four-value picture. Saturated red in the drink and the whole fruit; saturated fresh green in the leaves, the rinds and the calyxes; clear white in the ice, the pith and the surface; and pale neutral grey in the background. The red must stay a true strawberry red and never drift toward orange or magenta, and the green must stay fresh and never dull toward olive. The greys and whites are genuinely neutral and pick up no cast from the fruit around them — that contrast between the saturated food and the neutral ground is what makes the drink read as fresh. There is no blue, no yellow and no warm tint anywhere outside the food.

CAPTURE — A real exposure made on a full-frame camera with studio strobe. Light falls off gently toward the four corners. The bright edges of the ice cubes, the speculars on the condensation beads and the caustics through the citrus clip hard and stay very small; the bands on the cup wall and the reflection on the dome clip softly and keep their shape. Shadows stay open — the contact shadow under the cup holds tone rather than going black, and the darkest area of the background sits well above pure black. Every repeated element varies: no two strawberries the same size, shape or rotation, no two ice cubes identical, no two condensation beads equal, no two leaves the same, and none of them evenly spaced. Very slight fine grain throughout.

FINAL CHECK — One cup with a domed lid, alone, standing centred and spanning about seven tenths of the frame height on a white surface against a plain pale grey background, with nothing else on the table. Whole fruit, cut fruit, leaves and ice cubes are suspended in the air around it at four different distances, at different sizes and at different degrees of sharpness — the piece at the bottom left corner clearly larger and out of focus — none of them touching the cup and none overlapping its front face. The layering inside the cup is visible and irregular. All blur is depth-of-field blur; nothing is motion-streaked. Do not let anything cover the front of the cup and do not space the floating items evenly.

title: Cerveja gelada e linguiça quente: combinação perfeita!
description: Uma caneca de chopp gelado com a palavra 'Cheers!' e uma porção de linguiças fumegantes em uma chapa de ferro sobre a mesa de um restaurante.
prompt:
SWAP SLOT 1 — THE DISH. Image 1 is the food reference. Take from it only the food itself: what it is, how it is cut, how it is piled, its colours, and how far it is cooked. Take nothing else from image 1 — not its background, not its board or pan, not its surface, not its lighting, not its shadows, not its angle, not its colour grade. The dish is placed into the scene described below and lit by the lights described below.

To change the dish by text instead, replace what is named in the FOOD block, but keep the two rules that make it work. First, every element gets its own optical behaviour: whether it is wet or dry, matte or glossy, whether its cut face differs from its outer surface, and whether it is charred, caramelised or pale. Second, keep the architecture: a loose irregular heap on a dark hot pan, pieces at different angles with some tipped to show their cut faces and some showing only their outsides, never arranged in rows and never evenly spaced.

SWAP SLOT 2 — THE GLASS AND ITS MARK. The beer mug carries a short printed mark on its front. Take the wording, lettering style and colour of that mark from image 1 exactly as printed; the text below never invents any lettering. If no reference is supplied, keep the mark to a single short word in a white script, small and secondary, sitting on the upper third of the glass front. Everything else about the glass — its shape, its frost, the beer and the foam — is built from the text below.

THE PICTURE — A vertical close food and drink photograph taken in a warm dimly lit restaurant: a heap of hot grilled sausage on a black cast-iron plate set into a wooden board, steam rising from it, and beside it a heavily frosted glass beer mug full of pale golden beer with a thick white head, on a dark wooden table, with the room dissolved out of focus behind.

THE READING — This is a bar hero shot and it sells two sensations at once: heat and cold, standing side by side. The steam rising from the pan says the food came out of the kitchen seconds ago. The frost caked on the glass says the beer came out of the freezer. Neither works without the other, and the whole picture exists to put them in the same frame. The camera is low, near the level of the tabletop, so the mug stands tall in profile and the food is seen across its surface rather than from above — a drinker's eye rather than a photographer's. The room behind is present but never resolved: pendant lights, a banquette, tables and chairs, all reduced to warm blur, so the setting is implied and the two lit objects on the table are the only things in focus. And the food is heaped rather than arranged, which is what makes it read as served rather than styled.

FRAMING AND CAMERA — Aspect ratio 4:5, vertical. The mug stands on the right: its body occupies from about six tenths of the frame width to about nine tenths, its handle reaching almost to the right edge, its foam crown at about half the frame height and its base at about nine tenths of the frame height, so it spans roughly the lower half of the picture and is the tallest object in the frame. The wooden board runs in from the left: it crosses the left edge of the frame and continues past it, its far edge at about two thirds of the frame height and its near edge at about nine tenths, and its right end passes behind the mug. The black iron plate sits recessed in the board, and the heap of food on it occupies from about one sixth to about three fifths of the frame width, at about three fifths of the frame height. Behind and left of the food, a napkin holder stands at about one quarter of the frame width and half the frame height. Steam rises from the food through the upper middle of the frame. Everything above the far edge of the table — roughly the upper half of the picture — is the out-of-focus room. Lens 85mm, camera low, about twenty degrees above the plane of the tabletop, so the mug is seen almost in profile and the food is seen across its surface. Aperture f/2.8.

HERO EFFECT ONE — THE BEER AND THE FROSTED GLASS. Three separate materials stacked in one object, and each behaves differently.

The frost is the outermost layer: a fine crystalline bloom covering the outside of the glass, matte and light-scattering so it reads as an opaque white veil rather than as transparency. It is thickest and whitest around the base and along the handle, thins as it rises, and is patchier near the rim. Where it is thick, the beer behind it is not seen directly but glows through it as a soft diffused amber; where it is thin, the liquid shows more clearly. Running down through the frost are a few clear tracks and larger condensation droplets, each droplet a small lens with a bright rim, a darker core and one hard white specular on its upper side, and they vary in size and cluster irregularly rather than sitting in an even array.

The beer inside is a pale transparent gold and it glows because light passes through it: it is lighter and brighter where the path through the liquid is shortest, near the outer curve of the glass, and deepens toward a richer amber through the thickest part. Rising through it are strings of small bubbles, released from a few separate points on the inner wall rather than from everywhere at once, so they form three or four distinct rising columns; the bubbles grow slightly larger as they rise and the columns wander rather than running straight. The glass is moulded with vertical panels around its lower body, and each panel catches its own separate reflection and its own edge of concentrated light, so the base of the mug reads as a set of bright vertical bands. The thick base acts as a lens, pooling a brighter patch of light just above the tabletop.

The head is the third material: a dense white foam standing proud above the rim in a slightly domed crown, taller at the back than the front. Its surface is not smooth — it is finely cratered and irregular, made of tiny bubbles packed together, with slightly larger bubbles around its outer edge where it meets the glass, and one or two shallow dips in its surface. It clings to the inside of the glass in a thin ring just below the rim. It is the brightest and the only pure white thing in the picture, and it must clip softly and keep its texture rather than blowing out into a flat white shape.

HERO EFFECT TWO — THE STEAM. Thin pale vapour rising from the hot food, and the rule that governs it is this: steam is only visible where it passes in front of something dark. Against the dark banquette and the shadowed parts of the room it reads clearly as pale grey-white; where it drifts across a bright area of the background it disappears almost completely, and it must not be drawn as a solid shape floating over everything. It leaves the food as two or three separate narrow threads, denser and slightly more opaque close to the pan, and rises about a third of the frame height, curling and folding over itself, splitting into finer strands, wavering sideways rather than going straight up, and thinning to nothing near the top. Its edges are soft and feathered everywhere. It is frozen by the exposure — it holds internal curl and structure and is not dragged or streaked in any direction — and it never obscures the food beneath it or crosses the mug.

FOOD — A loose heap of grilled sausage cut into thick diagonal slices and short chunks, piled unevenly with some pieces tipped to show their cut faces and others showing only their curved outsides, some resting on top of others and the heap higher at one side than the other. The cut faces show a coarse interior in warm pink-red with irregular white flecks of fat scattered through it, and their outer edges are browned and caramelised to a deeper red-brown. The casing on the outside is shrunken and slightly wrinkled, taut over the meat, darker than the interior, with a few near-black char marks where it touched the hottest metal — irregular in size and placement, never evenly distributed. Every piece is wet with rendered fat, so each returns a broad soft sheen along its curve plus one or two small hard speculars where the fat has pooled, and a little clear fat has run down onto the plate and glistens there. A scattering of coarse salt sits on some pieces and not others.

PROPS AND OBJECTS — A rectangular cast-iron plate, matte black with a slightly pebbled seasoned surface that scatters light so it returns only a broad dull sheen along its raised rim and no highlight anywhere on its face, its two handle lugs visible at the left end. It sits recessed into a thick wooden serving board in honey-toned oak: the wood is smooth and finished satin, its grain running in long straight lines with a few darker streaks, its edges rounded and catching a soft continuous line of light, with a routed slot at one end. Behind and left of the food, a small metal wire napkin holder with white folded paper napkins standing in it as a triangle: the paper is completely matte, takes no shine, and is the brightest neutral surface in the left half of the frame, and the thin metal of the holder catches two or three narrow bright lines. Beneath everything, a table of dark stained wood with a satin finish, returning a soft broad reflection of the mug's base and a dim pool beneath the board rather than a sharp mirror image, with a diffuse contact shadow directly under the mug and under the board so nothing floats.

LIGHTING — Three systems. A soft key placed high and to the left and forward, raking across the food: it puts the sheen on every sausage piece, gives each one its own small shadow on the side away from it, and lights the napkins. A second source behind and to the right of the mug, passing through the beer so the liquid glows from within and the foam is rimmed brightly at its upper edge — this is what makes the drink read as luminous rather than as a solid object. And the room's own warm practical lights in the background, which own the amber glow behind and light nothing on the table. The foam is the brightest thing in the frame; the beer sits about a stop below it; the food about a stop and a half below that; the iron plate about three stops down and the table about three and a half, with the darkest corners of the room around four. Every transition curves with the surface it crosses; nothing is straight-edged. The lighting sets brightness and falloff only.

BACKGROUND — A warm restaurant interior, completely out of focus, with no readable detail anywhere. Behind the table, the padded back of a leather banquette running across the left half as a long dark band. Above and beyond it: two or three pendant lamps hanging at different heights, each rendered as a soft glowing sphere with a bright core and a warm halo, none the same size; a slatted vertical wood screen reduced to soft alternating bands; a small green plant at the top left as a cluster of soft dark green shapes; a bright doorway or further room on the right with warm wall lights washing down a pale wall; and beyond it a scatter of small tables and dark chair backs, their shapes readable but their edges dissolved. One small patch of cool blue-green light from a screen sits low in the middle distance, the only cool note in the room. Depth is carried by five separations at five distances: the board and food, the mug, the napkin holder, the banquette, and the far room.

FOCUS — Depth-of-field blur only, no motion blur anywhere; every edge is a still edge, the steam is frozen and the bubbles are frozen. If a different product calls for a different surface, substitute it, but describe the replacement the same way: what the material is, how polished or how rough it is, what it reflects and how sharply, and how the light rakes across it. Never name a surface without giving its optical behaviour.

THE PICTURE — A vertical product photograph of a single spirits bottle, alone, standing on a slab of dark polished stone in a black space, lit from behind so the liquid inside glows, with curling smoke drifting through the darkness around and behind it.

THE READING — This is a commercial product photograph built to make one bottle look old, warm and scarce, and every decision serves that. The strongest light is behind the bottle, so the liquid itself becomes the brightest thing in the frame and the product reads as the source of light rather than as an object being lit. Everything else is black: there is no set, no prop, no second object and no visible edge to the space, so the bottle is the only thing that exists. The smoke supplies volume and the passage of time, and the stone supplies weight and permanence — one says slow, the other says solid. And the label is the only matte, still, perfectly legible thing in a frame otherwise full of glow, movement and reflection, so the eye lands on it last and stays.

FRAMING AND CAMERA — Aspect ratio 4:5, vertical. Single object, centred: the bottle's vertical axis sits at about half the frame width. From the top of the closure to the bottom of the base it spans about four fifths of the frame height, its closure top about one eleventh of the frame height below the top edge and its base about one eighth of the frame height above the bottom edge. The bottle's body is about two fifths of the frame width. The stone surface begins at about three quarters of the frame height, running horizontally across the frame from edge to edge, and fills everything below that to the bottom edge; there is no visible far edge to the slab, no table edge, no wall and no horizon — the stone simply emerges out of the darkness. Lens 100mm macro, camera at about two thirds of the bottle's height, held level with no tilt so the bottle's sides stay parallel and the label faces the lens squarely without keystoning. Aperture f/11.

HERO EFFECT ONE — THE BACKLIT LIQUID AND THE GLASS. The main light is behind the bottle, so the liquid transmits rather than reflects, and the whole body of the bottle glows from within. That glow is not even: the colour saturates in proportion to how far the light has travelled through it, so where the path through the liquid is shortest — near the outer edges of the body — it reads a lighter, brighter gold, and through the deepest part of the bottle it deepens into a rich red-amber. The brightest zone sits toward the side the light comes from, and the far side falls into a deep warm brown. The glass itself behaves separately from the liquid. It is thick, clear and flint-coloured, and where the body curves round toward the sides it presents its greatest thickness edge-on, concentrating the light into two bright vertical bands running the height of the bottle, one much brighter than the other. Its base is thickest of all: it acts as a lens, pooling a bright concentrated area of light just above the foot and casting a warm caustic patch onto the stone in front of and beside the base. Above the liquid, the empty neck reads completely differently — clear glass and air rather than glowing colour — and the fill line where the two meet is a sharp bright horizontal band with a slight curve to it. Fine mould seams run down each side of the bottle and catch a thin bright line, and a few tiny bubbles are suspended in the thickest parts of the glass.

HERO EFFECT TWO — THE SMOKE. Separate from the glow, and never merged with it. Ribbons of pale grey-white smoke rise and curl through the black space behind and to both sides of the bottle, occupying roughly the upper two thirds of the frame. The smoke is lit from the side, so each ribbon is bright on the face turned toward the light and falls away to nothing on the other side, giving it visible thickness and direction. It is highly irregular: some ribbons are dense and near-opaque, some are so thin the black shows straight through, and they vary continuously along their own length. They curl into loose spirals and roll over on themselves, some drifting nearly vertically and others folding sideways, and where two streams meet they braid and tear rather than merging smoothly. The smoke is thickest and brightest in the upper left and upper right and thins out toward the centre so it never obscures the bottle's silhouette or crosses the label. Its edges are soft and feathered where it is thin and clearly defined where it is dense. It is frozen by the flash — the strands hold crisp internal structure and are not streaked or dragged in any direction. The labels are uncoated paper: their surface is fibrous and slightly textured, visibly matte, and they return no specular highlight at all, so they read a full stop flatter than the glass around them and their printed ink sits crisp and dark against the paper. The front label is lit clearly and evenly across its whole face so all of its printing is legible; the narrow strip label wrapping the side of the bottle catches the light at a steeper angle and is slightly brighter along its outer edge; the band around the neck is partly turned away and falls into shadow on one side. The paper edges are visible as thin bright lines where they lift a fraction from the glass, and one label edge is faintly deckled. Nothing overlaps the front label, no smoke crosses it, and no reflection washes over it.

LIGHTING — Two sources. The key is a hard warm-toned source placed behind the bottle and to one side, roughly at bottle height, aimed forward across the set: it is what drives the liquid's glow, what rims the far vertical edge of the glass with a hard bright line, what lights the smoke from the side, and what rakes low across the stone so the veining flares. Its shadow edges are crisp. The fill is a much softer source placed in front and to the opposite side, weak and broad, doing one job only — opening the front label so its printing stays fully readable — and it is dim enough that it puts no highlight on the glass and leaves the front face of the bottle otherwise dark. The brightest area in the frame is the glowing liquid near the key side; the label sits about two stops below it; the smoke about two and a half stops below; the stone surface about three stops below except where the veins flare. The space behind and above is unlit and reads black. Every transition curves with the surface it crosses; nothing is straight-edged. The lighting sets brightness and falloff only.

BACKGROUND AND SURFACE — Behind, a completely black space with no wall, no seam, no edge and no object in it, its only content the smoke drifting through it. Below, a slab of dark polished stone: the ground is a deep near-black with a faint mottled variation in it, and running across it are irregular veins of warm gold and ochre that branch, fork, taper and cross at unequal widths, some hairline and some as wide as a finger, never parallel and never evenly spaced. The stone is polished to a near-mirror, so it does three things at once: it returns a soft vertical reflection of the bottle directly beneath it, elongated and progressively broken up as it travels toward the camera; it catches the key light along the raking angle as bright streaks that run along the veins and make them flare much brighter than the surrounding stone; and it holds a tight dark contact shadow immediately beneath the bottle's foot, anchoring it to the surface. Depth is carried by four separations: the stone in the foreground, the bottle, the smoke behind it, and the black beyond.

FOCUS — Depth-of-field blur only, no motion blur anywhere; every edge is a still edge and the smoke is frozen rather than smeared. Critical sharpness sits on the front label — its paper fibres, its printed edges and its deckled edge are all fully resolved — and carries through the front face of the bottle and the fill line at the neck. The closure is very slightly soft. The stone immediately in front of the base is sharp, softening progressively toward the bottom edge of the frame. The smoke is soft by its own nature, softer the further back it drifts. The black space has nothing in it to be in or out of focus.

COLOUR — Three values and nothing else. Black: the space, the stone ground, the closure. Warm: the amber and red-gold of the liquid, the gold of the stone veining, and the warm cast of the key light. Neutral pale: the cream paper of the labels and the grey-white of the smoke. There is no blue, no green and no magenta anywhere in the frame. The blacks stay genuinely black rather than drifting warm, so the amber reads at full saturation against them, and the smoke stays neutral grey rather than turning gold.

CAPTURE — A real exposure made on a medium-format camera with studio strobe. Light falls off strongly toward the four corners, the upper corners darkest. Shadows stay open where they matter — the shadowed side of the bottle holds the shape of the glass and a trace of the liquid's colour rather than collapsing to black, while the empty space behind sits at true black. Every repeated element varies: no two smoke ribbons are the same density, no two veins the same width, no two highlights the same length. Very slight fine grain throughout, heavier in the dark background.

FINAL CHECK — One bottle, alone, standing upright and centred, spanning about four fifths of the frame height, its front label facing the lens square-on, fully lit and completely legible with nothing crossing it. The main light is behind the bottle so the liquid glows from within and is the brightest thing in the frame. Smoke curls through the black space behind and beside it, frozen and never streaked, and never in front of the label. Dark polished stone with gold veining fills the bottom quarter of the frame and returns a soft reflection of the bottle. Do not light the front of the bottle flat, do not let smoke cross the label, and do not add any second object to the frame.
